source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And he began{H2490} to speak{H1696} to them in parables and said{H559}: A man{H120} planted{H5193} a vineyard{H3754} and enclosed{H5462} it securely{H3190} with thorns{H329}, and dug{H2658} it out, and built{H1129} in it one{H259} tower{H4026}, and hired it out{H7936} to workers{H5647} of the ground{H127}; and he went{H1980} on a long{H752} journey.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses באטדים (ba'atadim, H329 'with thorns/brambles'). Greek has phragnon ('fence/hedge'). The Hebrew word atad appears in Judg 9:14-15 and Gen 50:10-11. A back-translator from Greek 'fence' would use geder, NOT atadim. The thorns foreshadow the crown of thorns placed on the son.
Uses עובדי אדמה (ovdei adamah 'workers of the ground'), echoing Genesis 2:5, 3:23. Greek has georgois ('farmers'). A back-translator would use ikkarim, not the Genesis-laden ovdei adamah.
Uses דמיונות (dimyonot 'likenesses/parables'), from damah ('to be like'). A natively developed Hebrew form.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'enclosed with thorns' (באטדים). Greek: 'put a fence around it'. Different enclosure.
textual_notes: The parable draws from Isaiah 5:1-7, preserving the same vocabulary.

verses.translation: And when he returned{H7725} at his appointed time{H6256}, he sent{H7971} his servants{H5650} to the workers{H5647} to take{H3947} the fruit{H6529} from the vineyard{H3754}.
And they seized{H8610} them and struck{H5221} them and sent them away{H7971} with empty{H7387} hands{H3027}.
Again{H5750} he sent{H7971} other{H312} servants{H5650}, and they wounded{H6481} them in the head{H7218} and shamed{H954} them.
Again{H5750} he sent{H7971} another{H312}, and him they killed{H4191}.

greek_deviations: Greek adds: 'and many others, beating some and killing some.' Hebrew is more concise.

verses.translation: And further{H5750} he sent{H7971} his son{H1121}, very{H3966} precious{H3368}, and said{H559}: Perhaps{H194} they will bear{H5375} honor{H3519} to my son{H1121}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יקר (yaqar, H3368 'precious/costly/rare'), consistent with 9:7. Greek has agapeton ('beloved'). Hebrew consistently uses 'precious' where Greek uses 'beloved.'
Uses ישאו כבוד ('shall bear honor'). Greek has entrapesontai ('will respect'). Hebrew: active honor-lifting. Greek: internal emotional response.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'very precious.' Greek: 'beloved.'
Hebrew: 'will bear honor.' Greek: 'will respect.'

verses.translation: And the workers{H5647} said{H559} together{H3162}: This is the heir{H3423}! Come{H935} and let us kill{H4191} him, and the inheritance{H3425} shall be ours.
And they took{H3947} him and killed{H4191} him and cast{H7993} him outside{H2351} the vineyard{H3754}.
Therefore what shall the man{H120} of the vineyard{H3754} do{H6213} when he comes{H935}? He shall destroy{H3615} those workers{H5647} and hire out{H7936} the vineyard{H3754} to others{H312}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יכלה (yekhaleh, H3615 'shall destroy/annihilate'). The word for total destruction (Gen 41:30, Deut 28:21). Greek apolesei ('shall destroy') is similar but lacks the annihilation weight.

verses.translation: Have you not read{H7121} this Scripture{H3791}: 'The stone{H68} which the builders{H1129} rejected{H3988} — it was laid{H5117} for the corner{H6438}'?

one_way_hebrew: Uses מונחת (munachat 'laid/resting'), from nuach (H5117). Greek egenthe ('became'). The stone 'rests' at the corner using the Sabbath-rest verb. A back-translator would use na'asetah, not the theologically loaded nuach.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'was laid for the corner.' Greek: 'became the head of the corner.' Hebrew lacks 'head.'
textual_notes: Quotes Psalm 118:22-23, a Hallel psalm sung at Passover and Sukkot.

verses.translation: And this was done{H6213} by our God{H430}; it is exceedingly wondrous{H6381} in our eyes{H5869}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'by our God.' Greek: 'from the Lord.' Hebrew uses personal possessive; Greek uses title.

verses.translation: And they wanted{H7521} to seize{H8610} him, but they feared{H3372} the people{H5971}, for they recognized{H5234} that he had spoken{H559} that parable about them; and they left{H1980} and forsook{H5800} him.
And afterward they sent{H7971} to him some of the Perushim and some of the men{H376} of Hordos, to catch{H8610} him on some matter{H1697}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אנשי הורדוס ('men of Hordos'), a Hebrew construct. Greek has Herodianon ('Herodians') a Grecized party name. A back-translator would transliterate, not create the native Hebrew construct.

verses.translation: And when they came{H935}, they said{H559} to him: Rabbi, we know{H3045} and recognize{H5234} you to be truthful{H571}, and you give{H5414} no heed{H3820} to any man{H120}; for you do not judge{H8199} by the face{H6440} of man{H120}, but show{H7200} the way{H1870} of HaShem{H8034} in faithfulness. Therefore tell{H559} us: Are we obligated to give{H5414} to Caesar, or not?

one_way_hebrew: Uses אינך שופט לפי הפנים ('you do not judge by the face') the Deuteronomic impartiality idiom (Deut 1:17, 16:19).
Uses חוייבנו ('are we obligated') Hebrew legal obligation term. Greek exestin ('is it lawful') asks about permission. Different legal categories: duty vs. permission.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Are we obligated?' (duty). Greek: 'Is it lawful?' (permission).

verses.translation: And Yeshua recognized{H5234} their falsehood{H8267} and said{H559}: Why do you test{H5254} me? Bring{H5375} me a coin and I will look{H7200} at it.
words: and I will look at it

one_way_hebrew: Uses פשוט (pashut 'a simple coin'), later Hebrew colloquial. Greek has denarion ('denarius'). A back-translator would transliterate dinar, not use Hebrew slang.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a coin' (generic). Greek: 'a denarius' (specific Roman coin).

verses.translation: And they brought{H5375} it to him, and Yeshua said{H559}: Whose{H4310} is this image{H8544} and the inscription upon the top{H1406}? And they said{H559}: Caesar's.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תמונה (temunah, H8544), the EXACT word from the Second Commandment (Deut 5:8, Ex 20:4). Caesar's image on the coin is framed as violating the commandment against images. Greek eikon ('image/icon') lacks this resonance. A back-translator would use tselem, not the commandment-loaded temunah.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'inscription upon the top.' Greek: epigraphe ('inscription'). Hebrew gives concrete physical description.
textual_notes: The use of תמונה creates ironic tension: religious leaders carry coins bearing a temunah while testing the Torah teacher.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: Return{H7725} to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God{H410} what is God's. And they stood{H5975} astonished{H8539} at him.
And the Tzaddukim came{H935} to him — those who say{H559} there shall be no resurrection{H2421} — and they asked{H7592} him, saying{H559}:

one_way_hebrew: Uses תחייה (techiyyah 'revival'), from chayah (H2421 'to live'). Hebrew focuses on LIFE; Greek anastasin on RISING. Different conceptual frame.

verses.translation: Rabbi, Moshe{H4872} wrote{H3789} to us, saying{H559}: If{H518} a brother{H251} of any man{H376} dies{H4191} and leaves{H5117} his wife{H802} without{H1097} a son{H1121}, the surviving{H7604} brother{H251} shall take{H3947} her as a wife{H802} to raise up{H6965} seed{H2233} for his brother{H251}.
Now there were seven{H7651} brothers{H251}. The first{H7223} took{H3947} a wife{H802} and died{H4191} without{H1097} children{H1121}.
And the second{H8145} took{H3947} her; he too left{H5117} no seed{H2233}. And the third{H7992} did{H6213} likewise.
And all{H3605} the seven{H7651} had her as a wife{H802}.
In the resurrection{H2421}, whose{H4310} wife{H802} shall she be, of all{H3605} these?
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: You err{H8582} and do not understand{H995} the Scriptures{H3791} or the power{H3581} of HaShem{H8034}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השם (HaShem 'the Name'), the distinctly Jewish reverential substitute for the divine name. Greek has tou theou ('of God'). A back-translator would write ha'Elohim, never HaShem.

verses.translation: When the dead{H4191} live again{H2421}, they shall not have wives{H802}, nor shall they have husbands{H1167}, but they shall be like the messengers{H4397} of the heavens{H8064} before{H6440} God{H410}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בעלים (be'alim 'husbands/masters', H1167). Hebrew explicitly addresses BOTH directions: women shall not have husbands, men shall not have wives. Greek is gender-asymmetric.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'not have wives, nor husbands.' Greek: 'neither marry nor are given in marriage.'

verses.translation: And concerning the dead{H4191} who shall rise{H6965} — have you not read{H7121} in the book{H5612} of Moshe{H4872}, when God{H410} appeared{H7200} to him at the bush{H5572}, saying{H559}: I am the God{H430} of Avraham{H85}, the God{H430} of Yitschak{H3327}, and the God{H430} of Ya'aqov{H3290}?

textual_notes: Exodus 3:6: 'I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'

verses.translation: He is not God{H430} of the dead{H4191} but of the living{H2416}; and in this you err{H8582} greatly{H3966}.

And one{H259} of the scholars drew near{H5066} to him — who heard{H8085} them debating{H3198} and recognized{H5234} that he answered{H6030} well{H2896} — and asked{H7592} him: Which commandment is the principal in Yisrael{H3478}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses העקרי (ha'iqari 'the principal/root'). Greek has prote panton ('first of all'). Hebrew seeks the root; Greek seeks the rank.
Adds בישראל ('in Yisrael'). Greek omits 'in Israel.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'which is the principal in Israel?' Greek: 'which is the first of all?'

verses.translation: And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559}: The principal commandment — Hear{H8085}, O Yisrael{H3478}! Your God{H430} — the Lord{H113} — He is one{H259}.

one_way_hebrew: The Shema (Deut 6:4). Uses אלהיך ('your God' 2nd person) vs. standard אלהינו ('our God'). Greek preserves 1st person 'our'; the Hebrew shifts to 'your' a teaching adaptation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your God' (2nd person). Greek: 'our God' (1st person).
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 6:4: שמע ישראל יהוה אלהינו יהוה אחד

verses.translation: Him you shall love{H157} with all{H3605} your heart{H3824} and with all{H3605} your soul{H5315} and with all{H3605} your mind and with all{H3605} your strength{H3581}. This is the principal commandment.

one_way_hebrew: Adds מחשבך (machshavtekha 'your mind'). Original Deut 6:5 has three: heart, soul, might. Both Hebrew and Greek here have FOUR. Hebrew uses מחשבה ('thought/plan') while Greek uses dianoias ('intellect'). Different cognitive concepts.
textual_notes: Deut 6:5: heart (לבב), soul (נפש), might (מאד). The Hebrew Gospels replace מאד with כח and add מחשבה.

verses.translation: And the second{H8145} is similar to this: You shall love{H157} your neighbor{H7453} as yourself. And no other{H312} commandment is greater{H1419} than these.
And the scholar{H2450} said{H559} to him: Rabbi, it is a great{H1419} truth{H571} that He alone is one{H259} God{H430}, and there is no other{H312} but He.

textual_notes: Echoes Deuteronomy 4:35: 'YHWH, He is God; there is no other besides Him.'

verses.translation: Him a man{H120} is obligated to love{H157} with all{H3605} heart{H3820} and with all{H3605} soul{H5315} and with all{H3605} strength, and to love{H157} his neighbor{H7453} as himself — and this is greater{H1419} than any human{H582} offering{H7133}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קרבן אנושי (qorban enoshi 'human offering'). Greek has holokautomaton kai thysion ('whole burnt offerings and sacrifices'). Hebrew has one compact phrase; Greek specifies two types. A back-translator would list two types, not compress to qorban enoshi.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'any human offering' (one phrase). Greek: 'whole burnt offerings and sacrifices' (two types).

verses.translation: And when he heard{H8085} that he answered{H6030} wisely{H2451}, he said{H559} to him: You are not far{H7350} from the kingdom{H4438} of HaShem{H8034}. And from then on, no man{H120} had the strength{H3581} to ask{H7592} him any question.
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and taught{H3925} in the Temple{H4720}: What do the learned scholars say{H559} — whose son{H1121} is he?

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Whose son is he?' (open question). Greek specifies 'the Christ is the son of David.' Hebrew omits, leaving it open.

verses.translation: David{H1732} said{H559}, prophesying{H5012} of him: The Lord{H113} said{H559} to my lord{H113}: Sit{H3427} at my right{H3225} until{H5704} I set{H7896} your enemies{H341} as a footstool{H1916} for your feet{H7272}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL - PSALM 110: Uses אמר האדון לאדוני ('The Lord said to my lord'). This preserves the crucial distinction: האדון (ha'Adon YHWH) vs. אדוני (adoni 'my lord,' the messianic king). Greek uses kurios for both, making the distinction INVISIBLE. Only Hebrew shows YHWH speaks to a human lord. This is a fundamental one-way marker.

Uses מתנבא (mitnabbe 'prophesying'). Greek has 'in the Holy Spirit.' Hebrew: prophetic act. Greek: spiritual inspiration. A back-translator would write b'ruach haqodesh, not the simple prophetic verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'David said, prophesying.' Greek: 'David said in the Holy Spirit.'
Hebrew: האדון / אדוני (two forms). Greek: kurios / kurio mou (same word). Distinction invisible in Greek.
translation_notes: אדוני (adoni 'my lord') is the KEY term. This is NOT Adonai (divine substitute) but adoni (human address). David calls the Messiah 'my lord,' distinguishing him from YHWH.
textual_notes: Psalm 110:1: Most-quoted OT verse in the NT.

verses.translation: If so, if David{H1732} called{H7121} him 'his lord{H113},' how is he his son{H1121}? And all{H3605} the people{H5971} heard{H8085} him with favor{H7522}.

one_way_hebrew: ברצון (b'ratzon 'with favor/delight'), from ratzon (H7522). Greek hedeos ('gladly'). Hebrew ratzon is the sacrificial acceptance term (Lev 1:3, Ps 19:15). A back-translator would use b'simchah, not the sacrificial term.

verses.translation: And Yeshua warned{H2094} them, saying{H559}: Beware{H8104} of the scholars who know{H3045} the books{H5612} — who desire{H2654} to wear{H5375} fine garments{H4403}, and that the merchants{H5503} give them greetings{H7965}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יודעי ספר ('who know the book') native Hebrew scribal description. Greek has grammateon ('scribes').
Uses הסוחרים (hasocharim 'the merchants'). Greek has 'in the marketplaces.' Hebrew specifies WHO; Greek specifies WHERE. A back-translator would write bashvakim, not 'the merchants.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'merchants give greetings.' Greek: 'greetings in the marketplaces.' WHO vs. WHERE.

verses.translation: And that they sit{H3427} in the first{H7223} seat{H3678} in the houses of assembly, that they be honored{H3513}, and that they be first{H7223} at the table{H7979}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בתי כנסיות (batei knesiyot 'houses of assembly'), the native Hebrew term for synagogues.

verses.translation: Those who uproot{H6131} the houses{H1004} of widows{H490} with the falsehood{H8267} of their prayers{H8605} — for this they shall suffer{H5445} a greater{H1419} penalty on the day{H3117} of judgment{H1779}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עוקרים (oqrim 'uproot'). Greek katesthiontes ('devour'). Hebrew: agricultural destruction. Greek: consumption. A back-translator would use okhlim, not oqer.
Adds ביום הדין ('day of judgment'). Greek has merely krima ('condemnation'). Hebrew adds eschatological Day.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'uproot houses.' Greek: 'devour houses.' Different imagery.
Hebrew: 'day of judgment.' Greek: 'greater condemnation.'

verses.translation: And Yeshua sat{H3427} before{H6440} [the treasury ark{H727}] where they deposit the treasure{H214} of the Temple{H4720}, and watched{H5027} how the people{H5971} gave their offerings there. And many{H7227} rich{H6223} people gave{H5068} great amounts.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ארון האוצר ('treasury ark'), same word as the Ark of the Covenant. Greek has gazophulakion ('treasury'). A back-translator would use otsar, not aron.
Uses מתנדבים (mitnaddevim 'giving voluntarily'), from nadav (H5068). The freewill offering term (Lev 7:16, 22:21). Greek ballonta ('casting'). Hebrew emphasizes voluntary nature.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'treasury ark.' Greek: 'treasury.'
translation_notes: [ארון האוצר] is bracketed, indicating editorial restoration.

verses.translation: And one{H259} poor{H6041} woman{H802} came{H935} and gave willingly{H5068} two small coins.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פרוטות (perutot), the smallest Jewish coin. Greek has lepta duo, ho estin kodrantes ('two lepta, which is a quadrans'). Greek gives BOTH Jewish and Roman equivalents. Hebrew uses only the Jewish denomination, no Roman conversion needed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'two perutot' (Jewish only). Greek: 'two lepta, which is a quadrans' (Jewish + Roman).

verses.translation: And Yeshua called{H7121} his disciples and said{H559}: Truly{H571} I say{H559} to you, that poor{H6041} woman gave willingly{H5068} more than all who gave abundantly; for this poor woman gave{H5414} all{H3605} her food{H3978}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מאכלה (ma'akhalah 'her food'), from ma'akhal (H3978). Greek has holon ton bion ('her whole livelihood'). Hebrew is concrete, she gave her FOOD. Greek abstracts to 'livelihood.' A back-translator would use chayyah ('her life'), not 'food.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all her food' (concrete). Greek: 'all her livelihood' (abstract).

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 12 in Hebrew contains several critical one-way translation markers. The most significant are: (1) אטדים (thorns, v1) vs. Greek fence — the vineyard enclosed with thorns that foreshadow the sons crown of thorns, using the OT word from Judges 9:14-15; (2) עובדי אדמה (workers of the ground, v1) echoing Genesis 2-3 adam/adamah pattern; (3) תמונה (image, v16) — the Second Commandment word, framing Caesars coin as idolatry; (4) אמר האדון לאדוני (The Lord said to my lord, v36) — Psalm 110:1 preserving the distinction between YHWH (האדון) and the messianic lord (אדוני), invisible in Greek; (5) קרבן אנושי (human offering, v33); (6) ארון האוצר (treasury ark, v41) connecting to the Ark of the Covenant; (7) פרוטות (perutot, v42) using Jewish coins with no Roman equivalent.
